title: Acute Pyelonephritis
subject: Medicine
summary: Acute pyelonephritis is a bacterial infection of the renal parenchyma and pelvis causing systemic illness and flank pain. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical signs and basic labs, with imaging when available.

sections.p: Infection that ascends from the lower urinary tract to involve the renal parenchyma, producing fever, flank pain and systemic signs.
b: Fever ≥38 °C, chills, rigors
Flank or loin pain with CVA tenderness
Positive urine dipstick for leukocyte esterase or nitrites

t.b: Does the urine show pyuria or nitrites? Positive indicates likely bacterial infection.
Is there systemic inflammation? Elevated values support infection.
Is there renal enlargement or loss of corticomedullary differentiation? Suggests pyelonephritis.

sections.p: Severity is judged by systemic response and organ dysfunction, using the Sepsis‑3 criteria.
b: Uncomplicated: fever, flank pain, normal vitals
Complicated: hypotension, altered mental status, renal impairment
Septic shock: persistent MAP <65 mmHg despite fluids

sections.p: Most cases are caused by ascending gram‑negative bacilli; in the tropics, additional risk factors modify the pathogen profile.
b: Escherichia coli (≈80 % of cases)
Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterobacter spp.
Enterococcus spp. in patients with urinary catheters
Candida spp. in immunocompromised (e.g., HIV CD4 <100)
Staphylococcus aureus from hematogenous spread (rare)
Tuberculosis of the kidney in endemic areas

sections.p: Patients present with a combination of systemic and local renal signs, often after recent urinary symptoms.
b: Fever, chills, rigors
Nausea, vomiting, anorexia
Flank or costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness
Malaise, confusion in elderly or immunocompromised
Possible dysuria or frequency (only ~30 % have lower‑tract symptoms)

sections.p: Targeted tests answer specific clinical questions; when a test is not available, use the next best alternative.

t.b: Is there pyuria or bacteriuria? Presence confirms urinary infection.
Is bacteremia present? Guides antibiotic choice if positive.
Is renal function impaired? Rising creatinine signals acute kidney injury.
Is there focal cortical involvement or scarring? Used for research or persistent cases.

sections.p: Identify patients at risk of rapid deterioration or long‑term damage.
b: Septic shock, persistent hypotension
Acute kidney injury (creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h)
Perinephric or renal abscess
Emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas‑forming organisms)
Progression to chronic renal scarring

sections.p: Start promptly with empiric antibiotics, then tailor; provide supportive care and monitor for complications.
b: IV fluids to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg; give crystalloid bolus 30 mL/kg if hypotensive
Empiric IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (covers E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus) – avoid aminoglycosides if nephrotoxic risk
If severe sepsis or shock, add IV metronidazole for possible anaerobes and consider carbapenem if ESBL risk
Switch to oral fluoroquinolone (e.g., ciprofloxacin) once afebrile and able to tolerate PO, unless resistance suspected
Avoid NSAIDs in acute kidney injury; use acetaminophen for pain/fever
Treat obstruction (catheter, stent) if present
In HIV with CD4 <100, consider broader coverage and monitor for opportunistic fungi

sections.p: Ensure resolution and reduce recurrence through patient education and addressing predisposing factors.
b: Repeat urine culture 48–72 h after starting antibiotics; ensure sterility
Assess for urinary obstruction; refer for imaging if pain persists >48 h
Educate on adequate hydration and timely treatment of UTIs
Screen for diabetes, HIV control, and sickle‑cell disease where prevalent
Consider prophylactic low‑dose nitrofurantoin in recurrent cases

sections.p: Conditions that mimic flank pain and systemic signs.
b: Renal colic from ureteric stone – usually severe colicky pain, hematuria, no fever
Acute appendicitis – right lower quadrant pain, not CVA tenderness
Perinephric abscess – may follow pyelonephritis, but imaging shows localized collection
Pyelitis – infection limited to pelvis without parenchymal involvement; milder systemic signs
Normal urine dipstick in early infection or after partial treatment – do not rule out pyelonephritis
Negative blood cultures do not exclude bacteremia; treat based on clinical severity
Ultrasound may miss early parenchymal inflammation – rely on clinical picture

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid rise in creatinine or signs of sepsis

faq.q: Can acute pyelonephritis occur without urinary symptoms?
faq.a: Yes, only about 30 % have dysuria or frequency; diagnosis rests on systemic and flank findings.

faq.q: Why avoid aminoglycosides in many patients?
faq.a: They are nephrotoxic and can worsen acute kidney injury, especially in dehydration or sepsis.
When the patient is afebrile, hemodynamically stable, can tolerate oral intake, and has no obstructive uropathy.

exam: What is the next immediate step for a patient with fever, CVA tenderness and systolic BP 85 mmHg? — Give a fluid bolus and start IV broad‑spectrum antibiotics.
How would you differentiate acute pyelonephritis from renal colic on bedside exam? — Presence of fever, systemic signs, and CVA tenderness versus colicky pain and hematuria without fever.

Why is ceftriaxone preferred over gentamicin as first‑line in most low‑resource settings? — Ceftriaxone covers the common gram‑negatives and is less nephrotoxic; gentamicin requires monitoring not always available.

A patient with HIV (CD4 88) presents with pyelonephritis; what extra considerations are needed? — Broader antimicrobial coverage for opportunistic pathogens and close monitoring for rapid deterioration.
What imaging modality would you request if the patient does not improve after 48 h of therapy? — Renal ultrasound to look for obstruction or abscess; if unavailable, consider CT if possible.
Explain why a normal urine dipstick does not exclude pyelonephritis. — Early infection or recent antibiotics can suppress pyuria; clinical signs remain decisive.
When is it safe to switch from IV to oral antibiotics? — After 48–72 h of defervescence, stable vitals, and ability to take oral meds.
What are the red‑flag signs indicating possible progression to emphysematous pyelonephritis? — Diabetes, gas on imaging, severe sepsis, rapid renal function decline.
